source: Dionysii Cartusiani Opera Omnia, t. II (Montreuil)

20.title: Expositio capituli vicesimi: Locutusque est Dominus cunctos sermones hos
20.title_en: Exposition of the twentieth chapter: “And the Lord spoke all these words”

paras.t: Jam datio legis describitur. Locutusque est Dominus cunctos sermones hos. In fine præcedentis capituli scriptum est, qualiter Moyses de celsitudine montis descendens, recitavit populo ea quæ ibi sunt scripta. Moyse itaque inferius exsistente cum populo, locutus est Dominus verba nunc exponenda, tam Moyse quam populo audiente, dicens : EEgo sum Dominus Deus tuus, qui eduxi te de terra Ægypti, de domo servitutis. Quemadmodum refert Lyra, Hebræi dicunt, quod istud sit unum et primum præceptum Decalogi, per quod affirmative præcipit Deus, ut ipse solus habeatur et colatur pro vero Deo, qui tam potenter et miraculose eduxit Israel de Ægypto. Quocirca Rabbi Paulus reprehendit Lyram, eo quod simpliciter narret prætactam Hebræorum opinionem, quasi probabiliter possit teneri, et non reprobet eam : quia si posset teneri, sequeretur secundum Rabbi Paulum, quod doctores catholici in enumeratione Decalogi deviassent a ratione. Verum hæc reprehensio est inepta, nec tenet consequentia illa : quia (ut infra patebit) etiam nostri doctores in modo numerandi, distinguendi, ac situandi decem præcepta, variis modis senserunt ; nec tamen hine sequitur, quod in hoc deviaverunt a ratione. Frequenter enim circa eamdem materiam diversæ opiniones possunt probabiliter teneri, absque errore et deviatione a ratione, quando non defenduntur cum incauta et temeraria assertione, ut patuit plenius in expositione exordii Geneseos, quod sancti doctores diversimode exposuerunt.
paras.en: Now the giving of the Law is described. [[20:1|And the Lord spoke all these words|Locutusque est Dominus cunctos sermones hos]]. At the end of the preceding chapter it is written how Moses, coming down from the height of the mountain, recited to the people what is written there. So, while Moses was below with the people, the Lord spoke the words now to be expounded, in the hearing of both Moses and the people, saying: [[20:2|I am the Lord thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.|Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus, qui eduxi te de terra Ægypti, de domo servitutis.]] As Lyra reports, the Hebrews say that this is one commandment, the first of the Decalogue, by which God commands affirmatively that He alone be held and worshipped as the true God, He who so mightily and miraculously brought Israel out of Egypt. For this reason Rabbi Paul censures Lyra for simply relating this opinion of the Hebrews as though it could be held as probable, without rejecting it: for if it could be held, it would follow, according to Rabbi Paul, that the Catholic doctors had departed from reason in their numbering of the Decalogue. But this censure is beside the point, and the consequence does not hold: for (as will appear below) our own doctors too have held various views on the way of numbering, dividing and ordering the ten commandments, and yet it does not follow that they departed from reason in this. For often several opinions about the same matter can be held as probable, without error or departure from reason, so long as they are not defended with incautious and rash assertion, as was shown more fully in the exposition of the opening of Genesis, which the holy doctors have expounded in different ways.

paras.t: Deinde Rabbi Paulus reprobat præfatam Hebræorum opinionem, quia in verbis his, Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus, non ponitur aliquod verbum imperativum aut præceptivum; sed est ibi solum denuntiatio quædam, qua Deus annuntiat populo quod ipse qui loquitur, sit Deus qui eos de Ægypto eduxit. Et in isto Rabbi Paulus catholice sentit, quia et Glossa ait: Non est istud mandatum, sed significatio cujus sit mandatum. Hoc idem asserit Augustinus et alii expositores communiter. Deinceps Rabbi Paulus tangit motiva Hebræorum, dicentium verba prehabita esse primum mandatum. Primum est, quia ad omnium divinorum observantiam præceptorum, necesse est præsupponere quod ille qui jussit ea, sit Deus qui Israel transtulit ex Ægypto : quoniam fides seu præsuppositio illa, est ratio obligandi ad servandum ipsius præcepta. Idcirco per verba hæc. EEgo sum Dominus Deus tuus, dicunt affirmative juberi, quod hoc firmiter credatur. Secundum eorum motivum est, quoniam antequam aliquis possit præcipere aliis, oportet ut recipiatur ab eis pro superiore. Ideo dicunt Deum primo jussisse per verba inducta, quod ipse haberetur ab Hebræis in Deum. Sed ista motiva quamvis aliquid contineant veritatis, non tamen concludunt propositumquia jam ante horum prolationem verborum filii Israel crediderunt, quod ille qui eos eduxit, esset verus Deus, et specialiter Deus eorum. Unde submersis Ægyptiis, cecinerunt : Cantemus Domino, gloriose enim magnificatus est. Quartodecimo quoque capitulo scriptum est, quod eis per maris fundum transductis, Ægyptiisque submersis, crediderunt Domino et Moysi servo ejus. Denique, præcedenti capitulo fassi sunt se velle esse subjectos imperio Dei, dicentes : Cuncta quæ locutus est Dominus, faciemus. Itaque Deus tanquam præambulum quoddam pramittens, locutus est populo Israel : EEgo sum Dominus Deus tuus, qui licet sim universorum Dominus atque Deus per creationem et gubernationem, conservationem et judiciariam potestatem, tamen sum specialiter Dominus Deus tuus, quem elegi mihi in populum peculiarem, et cui nunc legem et præcepta hæc tribuo.
paras.en: Next, Rabbi Paul rejects this opinion of the Hebrews, because in the words [[20:2|I am the Lord thy God|Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus]] no verb of command or precept is used; there is only a kind of declaration, by which God announces to the people that He who speaks is the God who brought them out of Egypt. And in this Rabbi Paul thinks as a Catholic, for the Gloss too says: This is not a commandment, but a statement of whose commandment it is. Augustine and the other expositors commonly assert the same. Rabbi Paul then touches on the reasons of the Hebrews who say that these words are the first commandment. The first is that, for the keeping of all the divine precepts, it must be presupposed that He who commanded them is the God who brought Israel out of Egypt; for that belief, or presupposition, is the ground of the obligation to keep His precepts. Therefore, they say, by the words [[20:2|I am the Lord thy God|Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus]] it is affirmatively commanded that this be firmly believed. Their second reason is that before anyone can command others, he must be accepted by them as their superior; so they say that God first commanded, by these introductory words, that He be held by the Hebrews as God. But these reasons, though they contain some truth, do not prove the point, because even before these words were spoken the children of Israel believed that He who brought them out was the true God, and in a special way their God. Hence, when the Egyptians had been drowned, they sang: [[15:1|Let us sing to the Lord: for he is gloriously magnified|Cantemus Domino: gloriose enim magnificatus est]]. And in the fourteenth chapter it is written that, when they had been led across the bed of the sea and the Egyptians drowned, [[14:31|they believed the Lord, and Moses his servant|crediderunt Domino, et Moysi servo ejus]]. Finally, in the preceding chapter they professed that they were willing to be subject to God's rule, saying: [[19:8|All that the Lord hath spoken, we will do|Cuncta quæ locutus est Dominus, faciemus]]. So God, setting this down first as a kind of preamble, spoke to the people of Israel: [[20:2|I am the Lord thy God|Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus]]; that is, though I am Lord and God of all things by creation and governance, by preservation and by power of judgment, yet I am in a special way the Lord thy God, thine whom I have chosen for myself as a peculiar people, and to whom I now give this law and these precepts.

paras.t: Consequenter exprimitur primum præceptum : Non habebis deos alienos coram me. Quasi dicat : Me solum pro vero Deo habebis, adorabis et coles ; omnes ceteros qui dii vocantur, refutabis adorare et colere per latriæ cultum, ita quod nec eos qui mendaciter dii vocantur, ut Jupiter, Mars, Saturnus, qui scelerati fuerunt, nec illos qui in Scripturis dii vocantur per participationem et gratiam, ut angeli et homines sancti, adorabis et coles latriæ cultu. Dæmones quoque a gentilibus dii mendaciter vocabantur. Corpora autem cælestia animata ponebant, sicque cælos, stellas, planetas, vocabant deos per quamdam participationem. De quibus in primo Timæi loquitur in persona Dei Plato philosophus : 0 dii deorum, quorum idem paer opifexque ego. Omnes hi possunt dii alieni vocari, in quantum per vitiosum cultum eorum homines alienantur, avertuntur et reprobantur a vero Deo: et item, quoniam Deus jussit, ut fideles sui ab illorum cultu se alienarent: rursumque, quia a vera deitate sunt alieni. Itaque ait : Non habebis deos alienos coram me, id est nullibi, quoniam ego ubique sum præsens, et cuncta intueor.
paras.en: Next the first commandment is stated: [[20:3|Thou shalt not have strange gods before me.|Non habebis deos alienos coram me.]] As if to say: Me alone shalt thou hold, adore and worship as the true God; all the others who are called gods thou shalt refuse to adore and worship with the worship of latria [the worship due to God alone]. So thou shalt adore and worship with latria neither those who are falsely called gods, such as Jupiter, Mars and Saturn, who were wicked men, nor those who in the Scriptures are called gods by participation and grace, such as the angels and holy men. The demons too were falsely called gods by the gentiles. And the gentiles held the heavenly bodies to be living things, and so called the heavens, the stars and the planets gods by a kind of participation; of these Plato the philosopher speaks in the person of God in the first book of the Timaeus: 'O gods of gods, whose father and maker I am.' All these can be called strange gods [dii alieni, literally 'alien gods'], inasmuch as by the sinful worship of them men are estranged, turned away and cast off from the true God; and again, because God commanded His faithful to estrange themselves from their worship; and again, because they are strangers to true divinity. Therefore He says: [[20:3|Thou shalt not have strange gods before me|Non habebis deos alienos coram me]], that is, nowhere, for I am present everywhere and behold all things.

paras.t: Non facies tibi sculptile, id est idolum aliquod ex quacumque materia, in qua sculpi potest. Et specialiter potest per idolum designari imago rei confictæ, quæ nullam exsistentiam habet, nec esse potest, quum dicat Apostolus : Idolum nihil est. Neque omnem similitudinem quæ est in cælo desuper, et quæ in terra deorsum, nec eorum quæ sunt in aquis sub terra : id est, nullam tibi formabis similitudinem per fusuram sive picturam cujuscumque rei creatæ, videlicet ad colendum aliquid tale, ita ut nec cælestium neque terrestrium neque aquaticorum imaginem tibi formes, aut fieri facias. Hinc subditur: Non adorabis ea neque coles, quia nec ipsam rem creatam, nec ejus imaginem. Aliqui namque putaverunt aliquid numinis esse in ipsis idolis, statuis seu imaginibus, ut Trismegistus, qui dixit : Statuas dico animatas sensu et spiritu plenas, imbecillitatem et sanitatem hominibus facientes. Aliqui vero hoc non credentes, coluerunt deos absque imagine eorumdem. Unde Varro, Valeriusque testantur, quod antiqui Romani deos diu absque imaginibus coluerunt.
paras.en: [[20:4|Thou shalt not make to thyself a graven thing|Non facies tibi sculptile]]: that is, any idol, of whatever material can be carved. And by 'idol' may especially be meant the image of a made-up thing, which has no existence and cannot exist, since the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 8:4|an idol is nothing|nihil est idolum]]. [[20:4|nor the likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or in the earth beneath, nor of those things that are in the waters under the earth|neque omnem similitudinem quæ est in cælo desuper, et quæ in terra deorsum, nec eorum quæ sunt in aquis sub terra]]: that is, thou shalt form for thyself no likeness of any created thing, by casting or by painting, for the purpose of worshipping any such thing; so that thou shalt neither form nor have made for thyself an image of things in the heavens, on the earth, or in the waters. Hence it is added: [[20:5|Thou shalt not adore them, nor serve them|Non adorabis ea, neque coles]]: neither the created thing itself nor its image. For some thought that there was something of divinity in the idols themselves, the statues or images; such was Trismegistus, who said: 'I speak of statues ensouled, full of sense and spirit, which bring sickness and health to men.' Others, not believing this, worshipped the gods without images of them; hence Varro and Valerius testify that the ancient Romans long worshipped their gods without images.

paras.t: Ego enim sum Dominus Deus tuus fortis, zelotes, id est, instar amatoris seu mariti aut sponsi zelotypi, volens solus amari et coli ut Deus et sponsus a fidelibus animabus : idcirco prohibeo eis fornicari cum diis alienis, quemadmodum sponsus non vult sponsam suam alteri commisceri. Qui autem accedit meretricem, non indignatur si et alter eam accedat, quia non habet ad illam amorem zelotypum qui socium et communicatorem excludit. Unde zelotes seu zelator nunc appellatur, qui sic vult solus amari, ita ut nihil secum ametur, in derogationem aut minorationem sui amoris. Sic igitur præcipit Deus se coli et honorari, ut ei dumtaxat tota mente adhæreamus, serviamus, atque vacemus, et non sit anima nostra dæmonum aut idolorum, alienorumve deorum adultera, sed Dei solummodo sponsa.
paras.en: [[20:5|I am the Lord thy God, mighty, jealous|ego sum Dominus Deus tuus fortis, zelotes]]: that is, like a jealous lover, husband or bridegroom, who wishes to be loved and cherished alone, as God and Bridegroom, by faithful souls. Therefore I forbid them to commit fornication with strange gods, just as a bridegroom will not have his bride joined to another. A man who goes in to a harlot is not indignant if another goes in to her too, because he has no jealous love for her, the kind that shuts out a companion and sharer. So He is here called jealous (zelotes, or zealous) who wishes to be loved alone in such a way that nothing be loved along with Him to the detriment or lessening of love for Him. Thus God commands that He be worshipped and honoured in such a way that we cleave to Him alone with our whole mind, serve Him and give ourselves to Him, and that our soul be no adulteress with demons, idols or strange gods, but the bride of God alone.

paras.t: Visitans iniquitatem patrum in filios, in tertiam et quartam generationem, eorum qui oderunt me. Non absolute ait, in tertiam et quartam generationem ; sed addit, Eorum qui oderunt me. Verumtamen additio ista, Eorum qui oderunt me, potest referri ad id quod dixit, Iniquitatem patrum, et etiam ad filios. Sed istud bonitati et æquitati Dei derogare videtur, ut iniquitatem parentum ulciscatur in sobolem, præsertim quum per Ezechielem locutus sit : Filius non portabit iniquitatem patris. Et per eumdem Prophetam ac Jeremiam : Omnis, inquit, qui comederit uvam acerbam, obstupescent dentes ejus. Nihilo minus idem Jeremias fatetur in Threnis : Patres nostri peccaverunt, et non sunt; et nos iniquitates eorum portavimus. Et in Josue leguntur filii Israel fugati, et quidam eorum occisi sunt propter peccatum Achan. Itaque circa materiam istam inveniuntur variæ auctoritates Scripturæ, quæ sibi invicem contrariari videntur. Nam et infra legitur, quod nunc in textu asseritur.
paras.en: [[20:5|visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me|visitans iniquitatem patrum in filios, in tertiam et quartam generationem eorum qui oderunt me]]. He does not say simply, 'unto the third and fourth generation,' but adds, 'of them that hate me.' Yet this addition, 'of them that hate me,' can be referred to what He said, 'the iniquity of the fathers,' and also to the children. But it seems to detract from God's goodness and fairness that He should avenge the iniquity of parents upon their offspring, especially since He has said through Ezechiel: [[Ezech 18:20|the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father|filius non portabit iniquitatem patris]]. And through the same Prophet, and through Jeremias: [[Jer 31:30|every man that shall eat the sour grape, his teeth shall be set on edge|omnis homo qui comederit uvam acerbam, obstupescent dentes ejus]]. Yet the same Jeremias confesses in the Lamentations: [[Lam 5:7|Our fathers have sinned, and are not: and we have borne their iniquities.|Patres nostri peccaverunt, et non sunt: et nos iniquitates eorum portavimus.]] And in Josue we read that the children of Israel were put to flight, and some of them slain, for the sin of Achan. So on this matter we find various authorities of Scripture which seem to contradict one another; and indeed what the text asserts here is read again below.

paras.t: Sed omnium horum solutio et concordantia ex dictis patet doctorum. Nempe, ut scribit S. Thomas in secunda secundæ, quod et ex dictis Alexandri de Hales habetur : Pœna potest considerari dupliciter : Primo, in quantum pœna, et prout per eam reparatur æqualitas justitiæ, dum peccator qui peceando nimis acquievit propriæ voluntati in derogationem justitiæ, aliquid patitur contra suam voluntatem, in ipsius justitiæ recompensam : sicque pœna pro proprio peccato infligitur. Secundo, consideratur pœna, ut medicina peccati, non solum curativa præteriti, sed etiam præservativa futuri, conservativaque boni : et sic aliqui puniuntur sine propria culpa, sed non sine causa. Per medicinam autem non est subtrahendum majus bonum, ut minus bonum obtineatur, sed econverso. Hinc aliqui absque propria culpa in temporalibus puniuntur per damna aut infirmitates, ut probentur, humilientur, aut alio modo gratiam sortiantur, sicque in spiritualibus bonis crescant, aut aliquo modo misericordiam consequantur. Nunquam tamen aliquis per spiritualium subtractionem bonorum punitur, nec in vita præsenti, neque futura, sine propria culpa. Sic ergo servi et filii in corporalibus aliquando puniuntur propter parentum aut dominorum suorum peccata, in quantum secundum corpus sunt aliquid seu res quædam illorum, ita quod parentes ac domini puniuntur in illis : unde in auctoritatibus dicitur, usque ad tertiam et quartam generationem, quia usque ad tot generationes vivere possunt parentes. Nec istud repugnat divine justitiæ, quoniam Deus hoc ipsum ordinat in ipsorum, sic patientium, bonum. Auctoritates autem contra hæc allegate, intelliguntur de pœnis spiritualibus et æternis.
paras.en: But the solution and harmonizing of all these is clear from what the doctors say. For, as St. Thomas writes in the Secunda Secundae [of the Summa], and as is also found in the words of Alexander of Hales, punishment can be considered in two ways. First, as punishment, inasmuch as by it the equality of justice is restored: the sinner who in sinning indulged his own will too far, to the detriment of justice, suffers something against his will in repayment to justice; and in this way punishment is inflicted for one's own sin. Secondly, punishment is considered as a medicine for sin, not only healing past sin but also guarding against future sin and preserving what is good; and in this way some are punished without fault of their own, though not without cause. But by medicine a greater good is not to be taken away to obtain a lesser, but the reverse. Hence some, without fault of their own, are punished in temporal things by losses or sicknesses, so that they may be tried, humbled or in some other way obtain grace, and so grow in spiritual goods, or in some way obtain mercy. Yet no one is ever punished by the withdrawal of spiritual goods, either in the present life or in the life to come, without fault of his own. So servants and children are sometimes punished in bodily things for the sins of their parents or masters, inasmuch as in the body they are something belonging to them, a kind of possession of theirs, so that the parents and masters are punished in them. Hence the authorities say 'unto the third and fourth generation,' because parents can live to see that many generations. Nor is this contrary to divine justice, since God ordains it for the good of those who suffer in this way. The authorities alleged against this are to be understood of spiritual and eternal punishments.

paras.t: Præterea Origenes solvit quæstionem hanc aliter, per patres peccantium, intelligens dæmones tentatores; per generationes, primam, secundam, tertiam et quartam, eos qui peccanti cooperantur, consentiunt, aut alio modo communicant.
paras.en: Origen, moreover, solves this question differently, understanding by the fathers of sinners the demons who tempt them, and by the first, second, third and fourth generations those who cooperate with the sinner, consent to him, or share in his sin in some other way.

paras.t: Et faciens misericordiam in millia his qui diligunt me, et custodiunt præcepta mea : id est, multo copiosius et protensius misereor posteris amantium me, et obedientium mihi, præsertim posteris prædestinatis. Nam ut ait Jacobus apostolus, Superexaltat misericordia judicium. Et Psalmista : Miserationes ejus super omnia opera ejus. Verumtamen in hac re attendere possumus, quam mirabilia et incomprehensibilia sint judicia Dei, quia interdum immediati filii justissimorum patrum sunt pessimi, et econverso. Ecce quam sanctus vir fuit Josias, et tamen filii ejus pessimi erant. Sic et Ezechias rex sanctus, filius fuit vitiosissimi Achaz. Denique, infra discutietur de ordinatione, enumeratione et situatione Decalogi ; et utrum dicta hucusque, sint ad unum præceptum spectantia, an potius sint duo præcepta.
paras.en: [[20:6|And shewing mercy unto thousands to them that love me, and keep my commandments.|et faciens misericordiam in millia his qui diligunt me, et custodiunt præcepta mea.]] That is, I show mercy far more abundantly and far longer to the descendants of those who love me and obey me, especially to descendants who are predestined. For as the apostle James says: [[Jas 2:13|mercy exalteth itself above judgment|superexaltat autem misericordia judicium]]. And the Psalmist: [[Ps 144:9|his tender mercies are over all his works|miserationes ejus super omnia opera ejus]]. Yet in this matter we may observe how wonderful and incomprehensible are the judgments of God: for sometimes the immediate sons of most just fathers are very wicked, and the reverse. See how holy a man Josias was, and yet his sons were very wicked; so too Ezechias, a holy king, was the son of the most vicious Achaz. Finally, below we shall discuss the order, numbering and arrangement of the Decalogue, and whether what has been said so far belongs to one commandment, or rather makes two.

paras.t: Sequitur aliud præceptum, et ut patebit, secundum in ordine. Non assumes nomen Dei tui in vanum : id est, nec falsum, nec sine rationabili causa jurabis per Deum. Nec enim insontem habebit Dominus eum, qui assumpserit nomen Domini Dei sui frustra : id est, talem tam inaniter jurantem, Deus non reputabit innoxium, sed transgressorem, damnationeque dignum ; imo decet ut nunquam sine reverentia et cordis attentione Deum nominemus, aut etiam nominari audiamus. Judæi vero affirmant hoc præcepto etiam prohiberi prolationem indebitam nominis Domini tetragrammaton, quod non licuit nominari nisi sacerdotibus, quando populum benedixerunt in templo.
paras.en: Another commandment follows, the second in order, as will appear. [[20:7|Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain|Non assumes nomen Domini Dei tui in vanum]]: that is, thou shalt not swear by God either falsely or without reasonable cause. [[20:7|for the Lord will not hold him guiltless that shall take the name of the Lord his God in vain|nec enim habebit insontem Dominus eum qui assumpserit nomen Domini Dei sui frustra]]: that is, God will not count one who swears so idly as innocent, but as a transgressor and worthy of damnation. Indeed, it is fitting that we should never name God, or even hear Him named, without reverence and attention of heart. The Jews, moreover, affirm that this commandment also forbids the improper utterance of the Lord's four-lettered name [the Tetragrammaton], which none but the priests were permitted to pronounce, when they blessed the people in the temple.

paras.t: Sequitur præceptum tertium : Memento ut diem sabbati sanctifices : id est, in sanctis operibus diem illum expendas, et divino cultui applices illum. Per quod aliorum dierum solennium, et nunc dominicæ diei jubetur celebritas. Instituit autem Dominus sabbatum, id est diem septimum, celebrari, in signum quod ipse die septimo requievit a cunctis operibus suis, et in commemorationem beneficii creationis, imo et aliorum Dei beneficiorum, quorum jugiter memores debemus esse. Propter quod præcepto huic præmittitur, Memento : quod verbum etiam ideo præmittitur, quoniam cum summa diligentia cultui est insistendum divino. Vel, ut asserit Rabbi Paulus, ideo verbum istud præmittitur, quia jam ante in descensu manna datum fuit istud præceptum, ut supra patuit. Recitat quoque Rabbi Paulus : Hebræi credunt quod sanctificatio sabbati præcipua consistat in corporalibus delectationibus ; traduntque quod quilibet tenetur in illo die ter manducare, videlicet semel prandere, et bis cœnare, atque quod omnes hoc facientes, sint securi a judicio gehennæ, ut in libro eorum de sabbato, expresse habetur. Ecce quam ridiculosum et stultum est hoc.
paras.en: The third commandment follows: [[20:8|Remember that thou keep holy the sabbath day.|Memento ut diem sabbati sanctifices.]] That is, spend that day in holy works and give it to divine worship. By this the keeping of the other feast days is commanded too, and now of the Lord's Day. The Lord instituted the sabbath, that is, the seventh day, to be kept as a sign that He Himself rested on the seventh day from all His works, and in remembrance of the benefit of creation, and indeed of God's other benefits, which we ought to remember continually. That is why the word 'Remember' is set before this commandment; it is set there also because divine worship must be attended to with the greatest diligence. Or, as Rabbi Paul asserts, this word is set before it because this commandment had already been given when the manna came down, as was seen above. Rabbi Paul also relates that the Hebrews believe the chief sanctification of the sabbath to consist in bodily pleasures, and teach that everyone is bound to eat three times on that day, namely to dine once and sup twice, and that all who do this are safe from the judgment of Gehenna, as is expressly stated in their book on the sabbath. See how ridiculous and foolish this is!

paras.t: Sex diebus operaberis, nisi in eorum aliquo aliqua solennitas occurrat, et facies omnia opera tua : unumquodque loco et tempore opportuno. Septimo autem die sabbatum Domini Dei tui est, id est, qui deputatus est cultui veri Dei. Non facies omne opus tu : id est, nullum servile aut mechanicum, præsertim nullum opus iniquum facies tu, id est facere tibi licet, et filius tuus et filia tua, servus tuus et ancilla tua, jumentum tuum, quia et pecora quæ laborant hominibus, voluit Deus tunc quiescere, convenienterque refici ; et advena qui est intra portas tuas, id est tibi cohabitat in villis, urbibus, aut domibus tuis. Et potest, per advenam intelligi quicumque ad Judaismum conversus. Deinde subjungitur ratio institutionis solennitatis sabbativæ : Sex enim diebus fecit Deus cælum et terram, mare et omnia quæ in eis sunt. Et requievit die septimo. Quod qualiter multipliciter possit intelligi, in expositione primi capituli Genesis diffuse expositum est. Idcirco benedixit Dominus diei sabbati, privilegiando eum præ ceteris diebus, et sanctificavit eum, id est divino eultui consecravit. Porro de expositione multiplici et plena intelligentia hujus præcepti et ceterorum præceptorum Decalogi, tot et tanta in aliis scripsi opusculis, imo et tanta inde habentur ubique, quod nequaquam stare intendo nunc in horum expositione hoc loco.
paras.en: [[20:9|Six days shalt thou labour|Sex diebus operaberis]], unless some feast falls on one of them, [[20:9|and shalt do all thy works|et facies omnia opera tua]], each in its proper place and time. [[20:10|But on the seventh day is the sabbath of the Lord thy God|Septimo autem die sabbatum Domini Dei tui est]], that is, the day set apart for the worship of the true God. [[20:10|thou shalt do no work on it, thou|non facies omne opus in eo, tu]]: that is, no servile or mechanical work, and above all no wicked work, shalt thou do; [[20:10|nor thy son, nor thy daughter, nor thy manservant, nor thy maidservant, nor thy beast|et filius tuus et filia tua, servus tuus et ancilla tua, jumentum tuum]], for God willed that even the beasts that labour for men should then rest and be suitably refreshed; [[20:10|nor the stranger that is within thy gates|et advena qui est intra portas tuas]], that is, who lives with thee in thy villages, cities or houses. By the stranger may also be understood anyone converted to Judaism. Then the reason for instituting the solemnity of the sabbath is added: [[20:11|For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, and the sea, and all things that are in them, and rested on the seventh day|Sex enim diebus fecit Dominus cælum et terram, et mare, et omnia quæ in eis sunt, et requievit in die septimo]]. The many ways in which this can be understood were set out at length in the exposition of the first chapter of Genesis. [[20:11|therefore the Lord blessed the seventh day|idcirco benedixit Dominus diei sabbati]], privileging it above the other days, [[20:11|and sanctified it|et sanctificavit eum]], that is, consecrated it to divine worship. As for the manifold exposition and full understanding of this commandment and of the other commandments of the Decalogue, I have written so much in other works, and so much on the subject is found everywhere, that I do not at all intend to dwell on their exposition in this place.

paras.t: Honora patrem tuum et matrem tuam, imo et ceteros progenitores, spiritualesque patres ac seniores, et benefactores ac magistros, cordiali affectu, decenti affatu, reali obtemperatione atque obsequio, et si opus fuerit, etiam sustentatione. De hac re infinita quodammodo dici possent. Subditur autem merces seu ratio hujus præcepti, ut sis longevus super terram, id est diu ac prospere vivas in terra. Non quod istud sit finale, principaleque premium observationis hujus præcepti, sed aliquantula retributio recte correspondens eidem : quoniam eum qui debite honorat principia suæ vitæ, puta parentes, decuit in ipsa sua vita prosperitatem et diuturnitatem sortiri, quemadmodum eum qui facit misericordiam, decet misericordiam consequi. Deus autem rudi populo veteris Testamenti temporalem promisit mercedem, ut vel sic ad obediendum alliceretur; tamen sub illa mercede subintellexit æternam ac spiritualem, quæ sola est premium condignum actuum virtuosorum, ex caritate Dei manantium, imo et ex actuali motione Spiritus Sancti. Unde quod ait, Ut sis longævus super terram quam Dominus Deus tuus dabit tibi,rite exponitur de regione cælestis patrie. De qua fertur : Credo videre bona Domini in terra viventium. Itemque : Beati mites, quoniam ipsi possidebunt terram : in qua justi sunt longævi, quia in æternum vivent in ea. Et quamvis prædicta secundum communem legem ita se habeant, quandoque tamen contingit occulto Dei judicio, quod honoratores parentum brevis et ærumnosæ sint vite, inhonoratores vero eorum, longeva ac prosperæ. Quod Deus sic ordinat ad majorem obedientium felicitatem, atque ad graviorem inobedientium damnationem. Vel ex aliis abditis causis id accidit.
paras.en: [[20:12|Honour thy father and thy mother|Honora patrem tuum et matrem tuam]], and indeed thy other forebears, thy spiritual fathers and elders, thy benefactors and teachers: with heartfelt affection, with fitting speech, with real obedience and service, and, if need be, with support as well. Endless things, in a way, could be said on this. Then the reward, or reason, of this commandment is added: [[20:12|that thou mayst be longlived upon the land|ut sis longævus super terram]], that is, that thou mayst live long and prosperously in the land. Not that this is the final and principal reward for keeping this commandment, but a modest recompense rightly answering to it: for it was fitting that he who duly honours the sources of his life, namely his parents, should obtain prosperity and length in that very life, just as it is fitting that he who shows mercy should obtain mercy. God promised a temporal reward to the unschooled people of the Old Testament so that by this, at least, they might be drawn to obey; yet beneath that reward He meant the eternal and spiritual reward, which alone is the worthy reward of virtuous acts that flow from the love of God, and indeed from the actual movement of the Holy Ghost. Hence His words, [[20:12|that thou mayst be longlived upon the land which the Lord thy God will give thee|ut sis longævus super terram, quam Dominus Deus tuus dabit tibi]], are rightly expounded of the region of the heavenly fatherland, of which it is said: [[Ps 26:13|I believe to see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.|Credo videre bona Domini in terra viventium.]] And again: [[Matt 5:4|Blessed are the meek: for they shall possess the land|Beati mites: quoniam ipsi possidebunt terram]]; in which land the just are long-lived, for they shall live in it for ever. And though by the common law things go as described, it sometimes happens by the hidden judgment of God that those who honour their parents have a short and troubled life, while those who dishonour them have a long and prosperous one. God so ordains this for the greater happiness of the obedient and the heavier condemnation of the disobedient; or it happens for other hidden reasons.

paras.t: Præterea, post præcepta ad Dei cultum spectantia, recte ponitur immediate istud de honoratione parentum, quia post Deum sunt præcipue amandi ac honorandi. Et sicut a Deo suscipitur anima, ita a parentibus contrahitur caro ; et ipsi post Deum sunt causa præcipua sobolis suæ. Quemadmodum etiam Deus est causa omnium, sic ipsi propria prolis.
paras.en: Moreover, after the commandments that concern the worship of God, this one about honouring parents is rightly placed immediately, because after God they are above all to be loved and honoured. And as the soul is received from God, so the flesh is derived from the parents; and after God they are the chief cause of their offspring. As God is the cause of all things, so they are the cause of their own children.

paras.t: Sequitur quintum præceptum : Non occides : id est, præcipio tibi ut nullum hominem injuste, seu privata et propria auctoritate occidas, imo nec lædas, neque percutias. Unde per hoc præceptum prohibetur omne in personam proximi nocumentum, præter juris ordinem irrogatum, juum hoc sit contra caritatem atque justitiam. Et sicut vetatur talis occisio, ita implicite præcipitur ordinata vitæ proximorum defensio aut conservatio, loco et tempore opportuno pro posse. Istud tamen præceptum, sicut et cetera quinque sequentia, respicit proximum, quantum ad mali evitationem.
paras.en: The fifth commandment follows: [[20:13|Thou shalt not kill.|Non occides.]] That is, I command thee to kill no man unjustly, or on thine own private authority; indeed, not even to injure or strike him. Hence this commandment forbids all harm done to the person of one's neighbour outside the order of law, since this is against charity and justice. And as such killing is forbidden, so the ordered defence or preservation of our neighbours' lives, in due place and time and as far as we are able, is implicitly commanded. This commandment, however, like the five that follow, regards our neighbour as to the avoiding of evil.

paras.t: Sextum præceptum est : Non mœchaberis. Per quod primo et maxime adulterium, deinde omnis illegitimus prohibetur concubitus. Septimum est : Non furtum facies. Per quod primo et evidenter inhibetur ablatio rei alienæ occulta, domino rei invito; deinde rapina quæ fit aperte ; omnis quoque injusta detentio, ablatio, et deterioratio rei alterius. Contra quod peccant, qui debita non persolvunt : qui et obligantur creditoribus ad recompensam pro damno, quod illi ex persolutionis dilatione incurrunt, si tamen persolutionem interim exigant. Octavum : Non loqueris contra proximum tuum falsum testimonium, nec in judicio, nec extra judicium : per quod omnis falsa accusatio, diffamatio, detractio, atque mendacium prohibentur.
paras.en: The sixth commandment is: [[20:14|Thou shalt not commit adultery.|Non mœchaberis.]] By this, first and chiefly adultery, and then all unlawful intercourse, is forbidden. The seventh is: [[20:15|Thou shalt not steal.|Non furtum facies.]] By this is forbidden, first and plainly, the secret taking of another's property against the owner's will; then robbery, which is done openly; and also every unjust withholding, taking or damaging of another's goods. Those who do not pay their debts sin against this, and they are bound to compensate their creditors for the loss the creditors suffer from the delay in payment, provided the creditors have meanwhile demanded payment. The eighth: [[20:16|Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour|Non loqueris contra proximum tuum falsum testimonium]], neither in court nor out of court. By this all false accusation, defamation, detraction and lying are forbidden.

paras.t: Non concupisces domum proximi tui. Hæc duo ultima præcepta, inordinatam appetitionem terrenorum restringunt ac vetant. Et nono isto præcepto inhibetur inordinata appetitio rei utilis, intelligendo per domum, quidquid ad possessionem seu opulentiam pertinet corporalem. Decimo autem præcepto vetatur concupiscentia rei delectabilis, utpote conjugis proximi, et omnis feminæ non conjunctæ legitime, quum dicitur : Nec desiderabis uxorem ejus. Porro quod subditur, Non servum, non ancillam, non bovem, non asinum, nec omnia quæ illius sunt, potest quasi per supplementum referri ad nonum præceptum, ita quod ista prohibentur injuste appeti ad possidendum et utendum eis in proprio obsequio, quod est bonum utile.
paras.en: [[20:17|Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house|Non concupisces domum proximi tui]]. These last two commandments restrain and forbid the disordered desire of earthly things. By this ninth commandment the disordered desire of a useful good is forbidden [bonum utile: a good sought for its use, as distinct from the bonum delectabile, a good sought for the pleasure it gives], understanding by 'house' whatever belongs to bodily possession or wealth. By the tenth commandment the desire of a pleasurable good is forbidden, such as one's neighbour's wife, and any woman not lawfully joined to oneself, where it says: [[20:17|neither shalt thou desire his wife|nec desiderabis uxorem ejus]]. What is added next, [[20:17|nor his servant, nor his handmaid, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor any thing that is his|non servum, non ancillam, non bovem, non asinum, nec omnia quæ illius sunt]], can be referred, as a kind of supplement, to the ninth commandment, so that these things are forbidden to be unjustly desired for possessing them and using them in one's own service, which is a useful good.

paras.t: Possunt quoque ad ultimum istud pertinere præceptum, ita ut intelligatur circa ea esse prohibita omnis concupiscentia bestialis et contra naturam. Verumtamen Origenes, Josephus et Hebræi dicunt, hæc ultima duo ad unum pertinere præceptum, quoniam de prohibitione utriusque concupiscentiæ loquitur textus iste permixtim, saltem secundum unam expositionem. Sed melior est Catholicorum distinctio. Nam alia est ratio boni utilis, et alia boni delectabilis ; et multi inclinantur ad unum illorum, qui ad aliud non afficiuntur, quemadmodum quidam libidinosi appetunt proximi conjugem, qui tamen furtum et rapinam abhorrent. Hinc etiam dantur diversa præcepta de refrenandis concupiscentiis, et de refrenandis earum effectibus. Insuper circa hæc Lyra recitat : Dieunt Hebræi, per hæc non prohiberi concupiscentiam, nisi aliqualiter prorumpat in actum exteriorem, videlicet concupiscentiam conjugis alienæ, nisi erumpat in osculum vel amplexum aut consimilia : cujus opinionis fuit et Josephus. Unde et quidam Catholici dicunt, quod lex vetus cohibuit manum, non animum. Sed Rabbi Paulus contra hæc scribit : Multi, inquiens, doctorum Hebræorum affirmant, per hæc prohiberi concupiscentiam alienæ uxoris aliarumque rerum, etiamsi in exteriorem actum non moveatur : et quod ita teneri oporteat, facile est probare, quum exterior actus rationem culpæ non habeat, nisi ex interiori deordinatione. Ratio quoque voluntarii, quod est origo meriti atque demeriti, primo et maxime invenitur in interioribus animæ. Denique in Deuteronomio habetur : Ne dixeris in corde tuo, Propter justitiam meam introduxit me Dominus in terram hanc : per quod prava et falsa cogitatio, et item presumptio prohibentur. Sed et in Levitico scriptum est : Ne oderis fratrem tuum in corde tuo. Et rursus: Nec memor eris injuriæ civium tuorum. Quod vero Catholici dicunt, intelligendum est, quod lex vetus non tam evidenter et frequenter cohibet animum, sed manum, præsertim quia non ita infligit pœnas temporales pro peccatis cordis, ut operis.
paras.en: These things can also belong to this last commandment, so that it is understood that all bestial and unnatural desire concerning them is forbidden. Origen, Josephus and the Hebrews, however, say that these last two belong to one commandment, since this text speaks of the prohibition of both desires mixed together, at least according to one exposition. But the Catholic distinction is better. For the nature of the useful good is one thing, and that of the pleasurable good another; and many are drawn to one of them who are not moved by the other, as some lustful men desire their neighbour's wife who yet abhor theft and robbery. Hence too different commandments are given about restraining desires and about restraining their effects. Further, on this Lyra relates: The Hebrews say that desire is not forbidden by these words unless it breaks out in some way into outward act; that is, desire for another man's wife is not forbidden unless it breaks out into a kiss or embrace or the like; and Josephus too was of this opinion. Hence some Catholics also say that the old law restrained the hand, not the mind. But Rabbi Paul writes against this: Many of the Hebrew doctors, he says, affirm that by these words desire for another's wife and for other things is forbidden even if it does not move to outward act; and that it must be held so is easy to prove, since the outward act has the character of fault only from inward disorder. The nature of the voluntary, too, which is the origin of merit and demerit, is found first and chiefly in the inward parts of the soul. Finally, in Deuteronomy we read: [[Deut 9:4|Say not in thy heart|ne dicas in corde tuo]]: [[Deut 9:4|For my justice hath the Lord brought me in to possess this land|Propter justitiam meam introduxit me Dominus ut terram hanc possiderem]]; by which evil and false thinking, and presumption as well, are forbidden. And in Leviticus it is written: [[Lev 19:17|Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thy heart|Non oderis fratrem tuum in corde tuo]]. And again: [[Lev 19:18|nor be mindful of the injury of thy citizens|nec memor eris injuriæ civium tuorum]]. What the Catholics say is to be understood thus: the old law does not restrain the mind so plainly and so often as the hand, especially because it does not inflict temporal punishments for sins of the heart as it does for sins of deed.

paras.t: Cunctus autem populus videbat, hoc est sensibiliter percepit et audivit, voces, id est tonitrua vel verba Dei prolata ex nube et igne. Solet autem in Scripturis visus pro quocumque exteriori accipi sensu, specialiter pro auditu, quemadmodum in Apocalypsi : Conversus sum, ut viderem vocem qua loquebatur. Et lampades, hoc est coruscantia fulgura, qui visu proprie sumpto percipiebantur, et sonitum buccinæ, montemque fumantem :sicut in expositione præcedentis capituli patuit. Et perterriti mente, ac pavore concussi in corpore sensitivaque parte, steterunt procul, non solum non transgrediendo terminos præstitutos, sed et retrogrediendo ; dicentes Moysi : Loquere tu nobis ex parte Dei, et audiemus auribus cordis ac corporis. Non loquatur nobis Dominus locutione ista sensibili terrifica, et per se seu per angelicam creaturam, ac forte moriamur ex nimia corporalis harmoniæ immutatione, atque formidine, ex nimiaque excellentia objectorum illorum, videlicet vocum ac fulgurum atque sonituum tubæ, per respectum ad nostrum auditum et visum. Nec potest humana fragilitas talia diu sufferre sine confortatione speciali et gratiosa.
paras.en: [[20:18|And all the people saw the voices|Cunctus autem populus videbat voces]]: that is, they perceived with their senses and heard the voices, namely the thunders, or the words of God uttered out of the cloud and the fire. In the Scriptures 'sight' is commonly taken for any outward sense, especially for hearing, as in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 1:12|I turned to see the voice that spoke with me|conversus sum ut viderem vocem, quæ loquebatur mecum]]. [[20:18|and the flames|et lampades]], that is, the flashing lightnings, which were perceived by sight in the proper sense, [[20:18|and the sound of the trumpet, and the mount smoking|et sonitum buccinæ, montemque fumantem]], as was seen in the exposition of the preceding chapter. [[20:18|and being terrified|et perterriti]] in mind, [[20:18|and struck with fear|ac pavore concussi]] in body and in the sensitive part, [[20:18|they stood afar off|steterunt procul]], not only not passing the bounds that had been set, but even drawing back; [[20:19|Saying to Moses: Speak thou to us|dicentes Moysi: Loquere tu nobis]] on God's behalf, [[20:19|and we will hear|et audiemus]] with the ears of heart and body. [[20:19|let not the Lord speak to us|non loquatur nobis Dominus]] with this terrifying, sensible speech, whether by Himself or through an angelic creature, [[20:19|lest we die|ne forte moriamur]] from too great a disturbance of our bodily balance and from dread, and from the overwhelming excellence of those objects, namely the voices, the lightnings and the sound of the trumpet, as they bear upon our hearing and sight. Nor can human frailty endure such things for long without special and gracious strengthening.

paras.t: Et ait Moyses ad populum : Nolite timere immoderato timore, vel quod nunc moriemini, sicut timetis. Ut enim probaret vos, venit Deus, hoc est, ob hoc per creaturam subjectam sic descendit, apparuit, atque locutus est Dominus vobis, ut ostenderet non sibi omnia cognoscenti, sed vobis ipsis ac aliis, quales sitis, et ut faceret vos probatos ac timoratos. Ideo subditur : et ut terror illius esset in vobis, id est timor filialis vel saltem initialis, et non peccaretis, quoniam timor Dei retrahit hominem a peccato. Stetitque populus de longe. Moyses autem accessit ad caliginem, in qua erat Deus, id est verticem montis ascendit, in quo fuit densissima nubes, in qua Deus per angelum apparebat, ut juxta petitionem populi mediaret inter Deum et eos in audiendo verba Dei, et referendo eadem ipsis.
paras.en: [[20:20|And Moses said to the people: Fear not|Et ait Moyses ad populum: Nolite timere]] with an immoderate fear, nor fear that you will now die, as you are afraid. [[20:20|for God is come to prove you|ut enim probaret vos venit Deus]]: that is, for this reason the Lord so came down, appeared and spoke to you through a created thing subject to Him, to show, not to Himself who knows all things, but to yourselves and to others, what you are, and to make you proven and God-fearing. Therefore it is added: [[20:20|and that the dread of him might be in you|et ut terror illius esset in vobis]], that is, filial fear, or at least initial fear [the fear of one beginning to turn to God, between servile fear and filial fear], [[20:20|and you should not sin|et non peccaretis]], since the fear of God draws a man back from sin. [[20:21|And the people stood afar off. But Moses went to the dark cloud wherein God was.|Stetitque populus de longe. Moyses autem accessit ad caliginem in qua erat Deus.]] That is, he went up to the summit of the mountain, where there was a very dense cloud in which God appeared through an angel, so that, as the people had asked, he might mediate between God and them, by hearing the words of God and reporting them to the people.

paras.t: Dixitque præterea Dominus ad Moysen: Hæc dices filiis Israel : Vos vidistis quod de ccelo locutus sim vobis, id est, sensibiliter percepistis verba prolata ab angelo, in mea persona loquente : quæ verba in cælo aereo sonuerunt, et cælesti virtute formata sunt. Porro de ista materia multa leguntur Deuteronomii quarto et quinto eapitulis, ubi inter cetera scribitur : Accessistis ad radices montis qui ardebat usque ad cælum ; erantque in eo tenebræ, et nubes, et caligo. Locutusque est ad vos Dominus de medio ignis; vocem verborum ejus audistis, et formam penitus non vidistis. Et accessistis ad me omnes principes tribuum, et majores natu, atque dixistis : Ecce ostendit nobis Deus noster majestatem et magnitudinem suam; vocem ejus audivimus de medio ignis ; et probavimus hodie, quod loquente Deo cum homine, vixerit homo. Cur ergo moriemur, et devorabit nos ignis hic maximus? Si enim ultra audierimus vocem Dei, moriemur. Quid est enim omnis caro, ut audiat vocem Dei viventis ?
paras.en: [[20:22|And the Lord said to Moses: Thus shalt thou say to the children of Israel: You have seen that I have spoken to you from heaven.|Dixit præterea Dominus ad Moysen: Hæc dices filiis Israël: Vos vidistis quod de cælo locutus sim vobis.]] That is, you perceived with your senses the words uttered by an angel speaking in my person; words which sounded in the heaven of the air and were formed by heavenly power. On this matter much is read in the fourth and fifth chapters of Deuteronomy, where among other things it is written: [[Deut 4:11|And you came to the foot of the mount, which burned even unto heaven: and there was darkness, and a cloud and obscurity in it.|Et accessistis ad radices montis, qui ardebat usque ad cælum: erantque in eo tenebræ, et nubes, et caligo.]] [[Deut 4:12|And the Lord spoke to you from the midst of the fire. You heard the voice of his words, but you saw not any form at all.|Locutusque est Dominus ad vos de medio ignis. Vocem verborum ejus audistis, et formam penitus non vidistis.]] And: you [[Deut 5:23|came to me, all the princes of the tribes and the elders, and you said|accessistis ad me omnes principes tribuum et majores natu, atque dixistis]]: [[Deut 5:24|Behold the Lord our God hath shewn us his majesty and his greatness, we have heard his voice out of the midst of the fire, and have proved this day that God speaking with man, man hath lived.|Ecce ostendit nobis Dominus Deus noster majestatem et magnitudinem suam: vocem ejus audivimus de medio ignis, et probavimus hodie, quod loquente Deo cum homine, vixerit homo.]] [[Deut 5:25|Why shall we die therefore|Cur ergo moriemur]]? [[Deut 5:25|for if we hear the voice of the Lord our God any more, we shall die|si enim audierimus ultra vocem Domini Dei nostri, moriemur]]. [[Deut 5:26|What is all flesh, that it should hear the voice of the living God|Quid est omnis caro, ut audiat vocem Dei viventis]]?

paras.t: Non facietis mecum deos argenteos, nec deos aureos facietis vobis, id est, nulla simulacra facietis,ut illa colatis mecum, vel per cultum latriæ, sicut adorandus et colendus sum ego. Unde et Samaritani et multi de regno decem tribuum, coluerunt simulacra sua seu vitulos aureos, et cum hoc Dominum adoraverunt, sicut nunc usque faciunt Tartari. Altare de terra facietis mihi, id est ad meum honorem. Hoc de altari holocausti exponitur, quia altare incensi fuit ex lignis setim, opertumque auro, ut infra habetur. In detestationem quoque idololatriæ jussit hoc Dominus, quia idololatre de pretiosis materiis faciebant altaria; et propter mysticam significationem, ad humilitatis commendationem. Et offeretis super illud holocausta et pacifica vestra per manus sacerdotum. Holocausta autem dicuntur, sacrificia quæ ad Dei honorem totaliter comburebantur ; pacifica vero, quæ pro remissione peccati, aut pro gratiarum actione de beneficio dato, aut pro beneficio obtinendo offerebantur,quorum una pars exstitit sacerdotum, una offerentium, ut comederent coram Domino,et tertia ad Dei incendebatur honorem. Oves vestras et boves, de quibus communiter sacrificia ista fiebant. In omni loco in quo memoria fuerit nominis mei, id est in locis specialiter deputatis ad hoc, ut in eis per sacrificia ista sit commemoratio et honoratio mei ipsius : quæ loca non fuerunt simul et semel plura, sed unus dumtaxat, in quo licuit oblatio talis, nisi forte ex dispensatione divina et causa idonea, sicut Elias obtulit in Carmelo. Successive autem fuerunt loca illa diversa, quia primus fuit in Silo, ubi tabernaculum fuit ad tempus ; deinde fuit in Nobe. Qua urbe per Saulem destructa, ut primo Regum habetur, in Gabaon est translatum ; postea in Jerusalem tempore David, ut patet secundo Regum. Verumtamen populus frequenter immolavit hinc inde in excelsis, id est locis sublimibus, prout in libris Regum et Paralipomenon recitatur : in quibus et hoc vituperatur.
paras.en: [[20:23|You shall not make gods of silver, nor shall you make to yourselves gods of gold|Non facietis deos argenteos, nec deos aureos facietis vobis]] [Denis's text reads 'you shall not make with me gods of silver']: that is, you shall make no images to worship them alongside me, or with the worship of latria, as I am to be adored and worshipped. Hence both the Samaritans and many of the kingdom of the ten tribes worshipped their images, the golden calves, and together with them adored the Lord, as the Tartars do to this day. [[20:24|You shall make an altar of earth unto me|Altare de terra facietis mihi]], that is, for my honour. This is explained of the altar of holocaust, for the altar of incense was of setim wood overlaid with gold, as is found below. The Lord commanded this also in detestation of idolatry, because idolaters made their altars of precious materials; and for a mystical meaning, to commend humility. [[20:24|and you shall offer upon it your holocausts and peace offerings|et offeretis super eo holocausta et pacifica vestra]], by the hands of the priests. Holocausts are the sacrifices that were wholly burnt in God's honour; peace offerings are those that were offered for the remission of sin, or in thanksgiving for a benefit given, or to obtain a benefit, of which one part went to the priests, one to the offerers to eat before the Lord, and the third was burnt in God's honour. [[20:24|your sheep and oxen|oves vestras et boves]], from which these sacrifices were commonly made, [[20:24|in every place where the memory of my name shall be|in omni loco in quo memoria fuerit nominis mei]]: that is, in the places specially appointed so that in them, through these sacrifices, I myself might be remembered and honoured. These places were not several at one and the same time, but only one, in which such offering was lawful, unless perhaps by divine dispensation and for a fitting cause, as when Elias offered on Carmel. But one after another the places were different: first it was at Silo, where the tabernacle stood for a time; then at Nobe; and when that city was destroyed by Saul, as the first book of Kings tells, it was moved to Gabaon; afterwards to Jerusalem in David's time, as appears in the second book of Kings. Nevertheless the people often sacrificed here and there on the high places, that is, on elevated spots, as is related in the books of Kings and Paralipomenon, where this too is censured.

paras.t: Veniam ad te, per gratiæ infusionem, et benedicam tibi, per infuse gratiæ multiplicationem, atque per terrenæ prosperitatis concessionem, si in cunctis obedieris mihi. Et in verbis his alloquitur Deus populum, tanquam quid unum, per Moysen. In veteri etenim Testamento temporalium bonorum affluentia promittebatur.
paras.en: [[20:24|I will come to thee|veniam ad te]] by the infusion of grace, [[20:24|and will bless thee|et benedicam tibi]] by the multiplying of the grace infused and by the granting of earthly prosperity, if thou obey me in all things. In these words God, through Moses, addresses the people as one single person ['thee', not 'you']. For in the Old Testament an abundance of temporal goods was promised.

paras.t: Quod si altare lapideum feceris mihi. Per hoc datur intelligi, quod altare de quo jam facta est mentio, poterat fieri tam de terra quam de lapidibus; sed de qualibus, subditur, non ædificabis illud de sectis lapidibus : id est, de lapidibus impolitis, non sculptis neque dolatis, volo id fieri. Si enim levaveris cultrum tuum super eo, id est, si eum ferro seu cultello preparaveris istud altare, lapides ejus secando, sculpendo, aut poliendo, polluetur, id est, contemptibile fiet, displicebitque mihi, eo quod factum sit aliter, quam præcepi. Causa litteralis hujus præcepti assignatur, quia idololatræ faciebant sua altaria de saxis sectis, politis, et sculptis : ideo in illorum detestationem Deus præcepit oppositum, et quia nolebat suos ministros communicare cum idololatris in divinis. Rursus, ne Judæi per talem sculpturam inducerentur paulatim ad sculpendum atque colendum imagines. Insuper ob mysticam significationem, videlicet quod Deus vult in spirituali templo suo (quod est Ecclesia) collocari personas integras et sinceras, unitatem spiritus conservantes, et ecclesiasticam unionem non violantes. Rursus, spirituale altare, est trium theologicarum virtutum connexio integra, in qua offerenda sunt Deo omnia opera bona et sacrificia militantis Ecclesiæ : quod altare fit de non sectis lapidibus, id est de tribus istis virtutibus firmis, ab invicem non divisis, nec alicui simulationi aut duplicitati adjunctis.
paras.en: [[20:25|And if thou make an altar of stone unto me|Quod si altare lapideum feceris mihi]]. By this we are given to understand that the altar just mentioned could be made either of earth or of stones; but of what kind of stones is added: [[20:25|thou shalt not build it of hewn stones|non ædificabis illud de sectis lapidibus]], that is, I will have it made of unworked stones, not carved or dressed. [[20:25|for if thou lift up a tool upon it|si enim levaveris cultrum super eo]], that is, if thou prepare this altar with iron or a blade, by cutting, carving or polishing its stones, [[20:25|it shall be defiled|polluetur]], that is, it will become contemptible and displease me, because it was made otherwise than I commanded. The literal reason given for this precept is that idolaters made their altars of cut, polished and carved stones; so God commanded the opposite in detestation of them, and because He did not want His ministers to have fellowship with idolaters in divine things. Again, so that the Jews might not be led little by little, through such carving, to carving and worshipping images. Moreover there is a mystical meaning: God wills that in His spiritual temple (which is the Church) whole and sincere persons be set, who keep the unity of the spirit and do not violate the Church's union. Again, the spiritual altar is the unbroken bond of the three theological virtues, on which all the good works and sacrifices of the Church militant are to be offered to God; and this altar is made of uncut stones, that is, of these three virtues held firm, not divided from one another, nor joined to any pretence or duplicity.

paras.t: Non ascendes per gradus ad altare meum : cujus jussionis subjungitur ratio: ne reveletur turpitudo tua. Ex quo elicitur, quod nondum erat tunc feminalium usus, quod infra patebit. Verumtamen si altare fuit tam altum, quod sacerdotes illud stando non valebant attingere, poterat pedibus sacerdotum scamnum aut aliquid tale supponi, quod facta ministratione removebatur, ut Magister in historiis tangit. Unde et Lyra allegat Rabbi Salomonem, dicentem quod fiebat ibi ascensus sine gradibus in hujuscemodi casu. Fertur quoque, quod in sacris Priapi sacerdotes per gradus ascendebant altare, atque in alto stantes, verenda sua monstrabant populo discooperta. Idcirco in tam obscenorum detestationem sacrorum, Dominus dedit præfatum mandatum. Spiritualiter vero per gradus ad altare ascendere, est, in fide superbeatissimæ Trinitatis, gradum et ordinem dignitatis asserere, affirmando quod Pater major sit Filio, et Filius major Spiritu Sancto, ut Ariani dixerunt : quod qui facit, turpitudinem suæ perfidiæ infelix ostendit. Rursus, altare de terra facere, est in Christo veram carnem fateri ; et ad altare per gradus non ascendere, est in eo divinitatem veram, qua æqualis est Patri, agnoscere.
paras.en: [[20:26|Thou shalt not go up by steps unto my altar|Non ascendes per gradus ad altare meum]], and the reason for this command is added: [[20:26|lest thy nakedness be discovered|ne reveletur turpitudo tua]]. From this it is gathered that the use of breeches [the linen drawers later prescribed for the priests] did not yet exist, as will appear below. Yet if the altar was so high that the priests could not reach it standing, a stool or something of the kind could be set under their feet and removed when the ministry was done, as the Master touches on in the Histories [Peter Comestor's Historia Scholastica]. Hence Lyra too cites Rabbi Solomon as saying that in such a case the ascent was made without steps. It is also said that in the rites of Priapus the priests went up to the altar by steps and, standing on high, showed their privy parts uncovered to the people; so, in detestation of such obscene rites, the Lord gave this command. Spiritually, to go up to the altar by steps is, in the faith of the most blessed Trinity, to assert a step and order of dignity, affirming that the Father is greater than the Son and the Son greater than the Holy Ghost, as the Arians said; and whoever does this, unhappy man, shows the shame of his faithlessness. Again, to make the altar of earth is to confess true flesh in Christ; and not to go up to the altar by steps is to acknowledge in Him the true Godhead, by which He is equal to the Father.

20.title: De mystico hujus capituli vicesimi intellectu
20.title_en: On the mystical sense of this twentieth chapter

paras.t: Quemadmodum quinquagesimo post exitum ab Ægypto die, data est lex Hebræis in monte Sinai ; sic quinquagesimo die post Christi resurrectionem, missus est Spiritus Sanctus primitive Ecclesiæ in grandi illo cœnaculo, in quo novissimam fecerat Christus Coenam : per cujus Paracleti infusionem, evangelica lex in Apostolorum, ceterorumque credentium cordibus est firmata, atque eodem die aliis in Jerusalem predicata et data, coruscantibus signis tanquam fulguribus, et apostolicis verbis sonantibus, velut tonitruis. Insuper, sicut Hebræis ex Ægypto salvatis data sunt decem illa præcepta immediate a Deo, id est non per Moysen, sed per allocutionem Dei ex igne et nube, tamen per angelum ; sic nobis ex mundi et vitiorum caligine per Christi adventum eductis, eadem præcepta sunt in Evangelio tradita, primo immediate a Christo Deo vero, veraciter incarnato, dicente : Si vis ad vitam ingredi, serva mandata. Itaque, non serviamus ultra peccatis, nec errorum ac passionum tenebris involvamur, nec alicujus idololatria immoremur caligini.
paras.en: As on the fiftieth day after the going out from Egypt the Law was given to the Hebrews on Mount Sinai, so on the fiftieth day after Christ's resurrection the Holy Ghost was sent to the infant Church in that great upper room in which Christ had made the Last Supper. By the pouring-in of this Paraclete the law of the Gospel was established in the hearts of the Apostles and of the other believers, and on the same day was preached and given to others in Jerusalem, with signs flashing like lightnings and the Apostles' words sounding like thunders. Further, as the ten commandments were given to the Hebrews, saved out of Egypt, immediately by God, that is, not through Moses but by God speaking out of the fire and the cloud (though through an angel), so to us, led out of the darkness of the world and of vice by the coming of Christ, the same commandments are handed down in the Gospel, first immediately by Christ, true God truly incarnate, who says: [[Matt 19:17|if thou wilt enter into life, keep the commandments|Si autem vis ad vitam ingredi, serva mandata]]. Let us therefore serve sin no longer, nor be wrapped in the darkness of errors and passions, nor linger in the gloom of any idolatry.

paras.t: Dicitur enim unicuique nostrum : Non habebis deos alienos coram me. Contra hoc agit superbus, qui se ipsum facit deum sibimetipsi, atque ab aliis tanquam deus vult honorari, dum non Dei, sed sui ipsius quærit gloriam et honorem; et ita se habet ac taliter gloriatur, quasi non Deo, sed a se ipso sit et habeat quod est, et quod habet. Magis quoque quærit sibi obtemperari, quam Deo. Nempe si videat Dei præcepta a se ipso ac aliis violari, non curat, nec contabescit, nec zelo inflammatur justitia zelando pro Domino, juxta illud: Tabescere me fecit zelus meus, quia obliti sunt verba tua inimici mei. Porro, si videat se contemni, aut propria vilipendi mandata, mox furit et indignatur, ac quasi sub colore justitiæ in contemptores sui exsurgit. In tali etenim homine improbo ac perverso, viget privatus amor sui, non sancta dilectio Dei. Quocontra ait Elias : Zelo zelatus sum pro Domino. Unde et Chrysostomus protestatur : Nihil iniquius quam Dei injuriam dissimulare, et propriam vindicare. O quam multi prelati ac principes sunt hodie tales! qui subditos suos per vitiorum abrupta proficisci conspiciunt, nec dolent, neque emendant, sed silent; propriam vero inhonorationem, nec in modicis rebus perpeti queunt: ideo non sunt veri vicarii Creatoris, sed servi ac filii dæmonis.
paras.en: For it is said to each one of us: [[20:3|Thou shalt not have strange gods before me.|Non habebis deos alienos coram me.]] Against this acts the proud man, who makes himself a god to himself and wishes to be honoured by others as a god, seeking not God's glory and honour but his own; he bears himself and boasts as though what he is and what he has came not from God but from himself. He also wants himself obeyed more than God. If he sees God's commandments broken by himself or by others, he does not care, nor does he pine away, nor is he inflamed with the zeal of justice, zealous for the Lord, according to that saying: [[Ps 118:139|My zeal hath made me pine away: because my enemies forgot thy words.|Tabescere me fecit zelus meus, quia obliti sunt verba tua inimici mei.]] But if he sees himself despised, or his own orders slighted, at once he rages and is indignant, and rises up against those who scorn him as though under colour of justice. For in such a wicked and perverse man a private love of self prevails, not holy love of God. Against this Elias says: [[3 Kings 19:10|With zeal have I been zealous for the Lord|Zelo zelatus sum pro Domino]]. Hence Chrysostom too declares: Nothing is more wicked than to overlook an injury to God and avenge one's own. O how many prelates and princes are like this today! They see their subjects going over the precipices of vice and neither grieve nor correct them, but keep silent; yet a slight to themselves they cannot bear even in small things. Therefore they are not true vicars of the Creator, but servants and sons of the devil.

paras.t: Similiter contra istud præceptum peccant avari, qui magis afficiuntur ad aurum, quam ad omnium fontem bonorum, qui nummum præferunt Deo, et pro pecunia relinquunt justitiam, ac lucri amore jurant, perjurant, fallunt ac mentiuntur, judicantque perverse. Propter quod divinus Apostolus avaritiam non inepte idololatriam appellavit. Rursus, contra idem præceptum agit luxuriosus, cujus deus venter est, et gloria in pudendis, qui fœdam carnem magis quam incomparabilem et superpræstantissimam Deitatem cogitat, amat, et adipisci conatur; et breviter quicumque in mortali est culpa, qui creatis magis quam Creatori, vanitati magis quam veritati ac æquitati inhæret, atque in his vanis, fœdis ac vilibus rebus finem sibi constituit. Iste sibi format et eligit deos alienos, de cujus vilitate ac impietate Sapiens ait : Cor iniqui cinis est et terra ; supervacua spes illius, et luto vilior vita ejus : quoniam ignoravit illum qui se finxit, hoc est, per debitum cultum non recognovit proprium Creatorem.
paras.en: Likewise the avaricious sin against this commandment: they are more attached to gold than to the source of all good things; they prefer money to God, abandon justice for money, and for love of gain swear, forswear, deceive and lie, and judge perversely. That is why the divine Apostle not unfittingly called avarice idolatry. Again, the lustful man acts against the same commandment, [[Phil 3:19|whose God is their belly: and whose glory is in their shame|quorum Deus venter est: et gloria in confusione ipsorum]], who thinks of, loves and strives after foul flesh rather than the incomparable and all-surpassing Godhead; and, in short, anyone in mortal sin, who clings to creatures more than to the Creator, to vanity more than to truth and justice, and sets his end in these vain, foul and base things. Such a man forms and chooses strange gods for himself; of his baseness and impiety the Wise Man says: [[Wis 15:10|his heart is ashes, and his hope vain earth and his life more base than clay|Cinis est enim cor ejus, et terra supervacua spes illius, et luto vilior vita ejus]]: [[Wis 15:11|Forasmuch as he knew not his maker|quoniam ignoravit qui se finxit]], that is, did not acknowledge his own Creator by due worship.

paras.t: Non facies tibi sculptile, neque omnem similitudinem, etc. Hoc præcepto jubemur cor nostrum a turpibus phantasmatibus, a sordidis phantasiis, a distractionibus, potissime orationis contemplationisque tempore, et in cunctis divinis purgare ac custodire, quatenus pura, ardente, ac stabili mente omnipotenti Deo simus intenti, ejusque opus cum debita reverentia jugiter persolvamus. Ego enim sum Dominus Deus tuus fortis, zelotes, visitans iniquitatem patrum in filios. Itaque si optamus ut anima nostra sponsa sit sui Creatoris ac Salvatoris, oportet nos ei indesinenter fidelitatem servare, nec aliquid nisi ipsum, vel propter ipsum, ac in ipso diligere, cordeque integro detestari ac fugere quidquid a mundissimis ejus amplexibus mentem avellit. Hinc sanctus Joannes apostolus loquitur : Si quis diligit mundum, non est caritas Dei in ipso. Et Jacobus sanctus : Quicumque, inquit, voluerit amicus hujus mundi fieri, inimicus Dei constituetur. Caveamus ergo ne vitiorum nostrorum filios, id est imitatores, consensores, cooperatores, aut quovis modo communicatores habeamus ac relinquamus : ne alios inducamus ad mala verbo, exemplo, aut opere : ne et nostra peccata in tertiam et quartam generationem visitentur a Domino, omniumque illorum peccata ac pœnæ redundent in nos.
paras.en: [[20:4|Thou shalt not make to thyself a graven thing, nor the likeness|Non facies tibi sculptile, neque omnem similitudinem]], etc. By this commandment we are bidden to cleanse and guard our heart from shameful images, from base fancies and from distractions, above all in time of prayer and contemplation and in all divine things, so that with a pure, ardent and steady mind we may be intent on almighty God and render Him His work continually with due reverence [opus, the 'work of God', that is, the Divine Office]. [[20:5|I am the Lord thy God, mighty, jealous, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children|ego sum Dominus Deus tuus fortis, zelotes, visitans iniquitatem patrum in filios]]. So if we desire that our soul be the bride of her Creator and Saviour, we must keep faith with Him unceasingly, love nothing but Him, or for His sake, and in Him, and with a whole heart detest and flee whatever tears the mind away from His most pure embraces. Hence the holy apostle John says: [[1 John 2:15|If any man love the world, the charity of the Father is not in him.|Si quis diligit mundum, non est caritas Patris in eo]] And St. James: [[Jas 4:4|Whosoever therefore will be a friend of this world becometh an enemy of God.|quicumque ergo voluerit amicus esse sæculi hujus, inimicus Dei constituitur.]] Let us take care, then, not to have or leave behind children of our vices, that is, imitators, accomplices, cooperators, or sharers of any kind; not to lead others into evil by word, example or deed; lest our sins too be visited by the Lord unto the third and fourth generation, and the sins and punishments of all of them redound upon us.

paras.t: Non assumes nomen Dei tui in vanum. Hoc est quod in Evangelio loquitur Dominus : Ego dico vobis non jurare omnino. Sit autem sermo vester : Est, est; non, non. Jacobus quoque apostolus : Ante omnia nolite jurare. Abjiciatur ergo detestabilis actus et pessima consuetudo, quum et in Ecclesiastico scriptum sit : Jurationi non assuescat os tuum, multi enim casus in ea. Vir multum jurans replebitur iniquitate, et non deficiet de domo ejus plaga. Nempe quum consuetudo venialium sit mortalis, quanto magis consuetudo jurandi enormiter vitiosa est atque mortifera, quum sine rationabili causa jurare sit contra divinum præceptum, ideoque ex genere suo mortale ?
paras.en: [[20:7|Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain|Non assumes nomen Domini Dei tui in vanum]]. This is what the Lord says in the Gospel: [[Matt 5:34|But I say to you not to swear at all|Ego autem dico vobis, non jurare omnino]]. [[Matt 5:37|But let your speech be yea, yea: no, no|Sit autem sermo vester, est, est: non, non]]. And the apostle James: [[Jas 5:12|But above all things, my brethren, swear not|Ante omnia autem, fratres mei, nolite jurare]]. Let this detestable act and most wicked habit be cast away, then, since it is written in Ecclesiasticus too: [[Ecclus 23:9|Let not thy mouth be accustomed to swearing: for in it there are many falls.|Jurationi non assuescat os tuum: multi enim casus in illa.]] [[Ecclus 23:12|A man that sweareth much, shall be filled with iniquity, and a scourge shall not depart from his house.|Vir multum jurans implebitur iniquitate, et non discedet a domo illius plaga.]] For if even the habit of venial sins is deadly, how much more is the habit of swearing grievously vicious and deadly, since to swear without reasonable cause is against the divine commandment, and therefore mortal in its kind?

paras.t: Memento ut diem sabbati sanctifices. Itaque diebus festivis summe tenemur abstinere a vitiis : ita quod si quis tunc detrahat, fornicetur, contendat, crapulamve committat, aut acediæ præbeat in se locum, vel quodcumque mortale incidat vitium, non solum committit unum aut simplex mortale peccatum, nec tantum transgreditur unum præceptum, sed duo ad minus; et duo incurrit peccata mortalia, aut unum dupliciter vel pluribus modis mortale. Quemadmodum etiam si aliquid horum committat in sacro loco, aut cum religiosa, seu in sacris Ordinibus constituta persona. Hinc et venialia, quæ ad mortale disponunt, tunc gravantur, ac magis vitanda sunt. Denique valde pensandum est quod Dominus jubet : Non facies oomne opus tu et filius tuus, et filia tua, servus tuus et ancilla, etc. Quo constat, quod parentes et domini domus, tunc præcipue obligantur sobolem suam atque familiam quantum congrue valent, et caritas exigit, a peccatis retrahere, admonere, et ædificare. Itaque quum sabbatum sit requies Domini, diebus celebribus conquiescat mens nostra in Deo quiete præcipua per devotionem internam, per orationes puras atque assiduas, per contemplationem sinceram, per amorem ferventem.
paras.en: [[20:8|Remember that thou keep holy the sabbath day.|Memento ut diem sabbati sanctifices.]] So on feast days we are bound above all to abstain from vices; so that if anyone on such a day detracts, fornicates, quarrels, gets drunk, gives room in himself to acedia [spiritual sloth], or falls into any other mortal vice, he commits not merely one simple mortal sin, nor breaks only one commandment, but two at least: he incurs two mortal sins, or one that is mortal doubly or in several ways. It is the same if he commits any of these in a holy place, or with a person in religious vows or in sacred Orders. Hence venial sins too, which dispose toward mortal sin, are then aggravated and are the more to be avoided. Finally, we must weigh carefully what the Lord commands: [[20:10|thou shalt do no work on it, thou nor thy son, nor thy daughter, nor thy manservant, nor thy maidservant|non facies omne opus in eo, tu, et filius tuus et filia tua, servus tuus et ancilla tua]], etc. From this it is clear that parents and heads of households are then especially bound, as far as they fittingly can and as charity requires, to draw their children and household away from sin, to admonish and to edify them. And so, since the sabbath is the Lord's rest, on feast days let our mind rest in God with a special quiet, through inward devotion, through pure and constant prayers, through sincere contemplation, through fervent love.

paras.t: Honora patrem tuum et matrem tuam. Omnis igitur Christifidelis superioribus suis tanquam Dei vicariis debitam subjectionem, reverentiam cordialem, obedientiam exhibeat promptam.
paras.en: [[20:12|Honour thy father and thy mother|Honora patrem tuum et matrem tuam]]. Let every one of Christ's faithful, then, show his superiors, as the vicars of God, due subjection, heartfelt reverence and prompt obedience.

paras.t: Stetitque populus de longe, Moyses autem accessit ad caliginem, in qua erat Deus. Hanc clausulam magnus et theologissimus Dionysius in libro de Mystica Theologia profundissime interpretatur, intelligendo per Moysen, quemcumque virum heroicum ac perfectum, qui relictis ac supergressis omnibus sensibilibus ac intelligibilibus, imo universis creatis, atque se ipso et cunctis actibus suis, Deo per ardentissimam dilectionem unitur, intratque caliginem in qua vere est Deus. Hæc namjue caligo, est æternæ, increatæ, infinitæque lucis divine superexcellens, incomprehensibilis et superclarissima plenitudo, abyssalis, interminabilis atque supersimplicissima magnitudo, in qua Deus esse et habitare censetur, qui ponit tenebras (id est infinitam hanc lucem, omnem creatarum mentium capacitatem infinite transcendentem ac superantem) latibulum suum ; et ipsæ divinæ tenebræ cooperiuntur et absconduntur omni visioni ac lumini, ob incircumscriptibilem suam plenitudinem, prorsus impenetrabilem et immensam. Quum itaque mens æstuantissimo caritatis ardore succensa, Deo ita conjungitur per contemplationem theoricam et sapientiam luminosam, flammigeram, unitivam, dicitur introire caliginem, instarque Moysis ab omnibus separari. Unitur enim Deo tanquam prorsus incomprehensibili, et quoad quid est, mere ignoto: et tamen hoc ipsum sic intueri, est clarissime ac suavissime contemplari, speciesque altissima contemplationis huic vitæ possibilis. Ideireo tunc tota in lucem illam tam infinitam expanditur, increatæ veritati infigitur, superessentiali deitati et superbeatissimæ Trinitati tam radiose, amorose et proxime copulatur, quod aliud nihil advertit, nec proprium actum attendit, sed defluit a se ipsa, atque in proprium refluit fontem.
